notes: Actual results for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2025, as reported to the MA Division of Local Services on Schedule A, not a budget.

Includes public schools. Massachusetts cities and towns pay for their schools and their share of any regional school district through the town budget, where most other states have separate school districts, so spending and property tax per resident run higher than in those states.

Covers the general fund, special revenue funds (federal and state grants, school lunch, revolving and other special revenue), capital projects and enterprise funds such as water and sewer: $134,863,209 of revenue and $282,712,965 of spending outside the general fund. Trust funds, transfers between funds and borrowing are left out. Capital projects spent $177,735,490 more than they took in, which is generally paid with bonds. Fire, water and other districts inside the town are separate governments and are not included.
Debt is all long-term debt the town reported outstanding at the end of FY 2025 (Schedule A Part 10), including school construction and any water, sewer or other enterprise fund borrowing.
"Taxes" on Schedule A include motor vehicle and other local excises ($33,121,701), which are shown as other local taxes. The rest, with penalties and interest, is shown as property tax.
Left out: transfers in from the town's own funds ($67,094,005) and other financing sources such as bond proceeds ($775,000), which are not new revenue.

Fixed costs ($99,156,169: health insurance, pensions and other benefits for town and school staff) are spread across departments in proportion to their size, schools included, as with benefits in other states. Debt service is left out of that spread.
Intergovernmental assessments and other spending ($73,317,833: charter school tuition, regional transit and county and state charges) are spread across departments in proportion to their size.

Political money counts contributions from unions and registered PACs to Cambridge's party ward, town and city committees and its candidates for mayor and city council, filed with the Office of Campaign and Political Finance since 2023. Corporate contributions are banned in Massachusetts. Individuals and money passed between candidate and party committees are not counted. Candidates for other offices file with the city clerk, so their own committees are not included, and party committees also support state candidates.

Transparency: City of Cambridge has filed its Schedule A annual financial report with the Division of Local Services for FY 2025, the latest year most MA governments have filed. This is a check that the report was filed, not an opinion on its contents. The other five practices have not been checked yet, so they are left out of the score.

Cameras: 2 license-plate cameras are mapped inside City of Cambridge's borders in OpenStreetMap (0 made by Flock Safety), not counting cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies. Flock cameras count as a red flag whoever runs them. Other brands count only when the government is the recorded operator, since many have no operator recorded.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-18. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals and corporate tax breaks have not been checked for Massachusetts yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.
